title: Brandenburg Concerto No. 5 in D major
hook: The harpsichord, usually heard in the background, walks to the front and takes over.

painting.title: The Flute Concert of Frederick the Great at Sanssouci
painting.pairingNote: A flute, a violin and a harpsichord lead a Prussian court concert, with Bach’s son Carl Philipp Emanuel at the keyboard; the same three soloists Bach chose for this concerto.

facts: In 1721 Bach, then music director to Prince Leopold at Köthen, copied out six concertos in his own hand and sent them to Christian Ludwig, Margrave of Brandenburg-Schwedt, with a dedication in French dated 24 March. He had played for the margrave a few years earlier, probably in Berlin in 1719. Bach called them simply *Six concertos for several instruments*; the name “Brandenburg” was given to them later.

Each of the six uses a different group of soloists. No. 5 has three: a flute, a violin and a harpsichord, with a small string band. The harpsichord has two jobs at once: it is one of the soloists, and it is also the [[continuo|continuo]], filling in the chords under everyone else.

It was probably the last of the six to be written, perhaps to show off a new harpsichord by the Berlin maker Michael Mietke that Bach had bought for the Köthen court in 1719. Bach almost certainly played the harpsichord part himself.

The first movement ends with a long [[cadenza|cadenza]] for harpsichord alone, far longer than anything a keyboard had been given in a concerto before. Scholars see in this work the beginning of the keyboard concerto.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a bright race that ends in a huge harpsichord solo (I), a quiet conversation for three (II), a skipping finale that starts like a fugue (III).

movements.heading: Allegro
movements.summary: A firm, sunny refrain for everyone, the [[ritornello|ritornello]], returns again and again, while the flute and the violin trade ideas between its returns. Little by little the harpsichord’s running notes push forward, until everyone else falls silent and it plays alone for minutes on end.

mainIdeas.name: The refrain
mainIdeas.description: a bold tune for the whole group, built on repeated notes and a steady, striding bass.

mainIdeas.name: The duet
mainIdeas.description: the flute and the violin pass a short rising figure back and forth.

mainIdeas.name: The harpsichord’s runs
mainIdeas.description: quick, unbroken streams of notes in the right hand, first as decoration, then as the main event.

stops.hear: Everyone plays a confident tune on repeated notes; the harpsichord’s chords glitter inside the sound
The band drops back; the flute and the violin answer each other, and the harpsichord adds fast running notes
stops.happening: The first solo episode for the three soloists

stops.hear: The refrain returns briefly, in a new key
stops.happening: The ritornello comes back in fragments between the episodes

stops.hear: Quieter and darker: the flute and the violin exchange short, gentle phrases over soft repeated notes
stops.happening: The central episode, in a minor key

stops.hear: The harpsichord’s runs grow longer and louder; the flute and the violin play less and less
stops.happening: The harpsichord starts to take over

stops.hear: Everyone else stops. The harpsichord plays on alone
Fast scales across the whole keyboard, then a long passage in which the two hands alternate rapidly, building up and up
The whole group comes back in with the opening refrain

notice: Follow the harpsichord from the start. At first it is just chords in the background; listen for the moment when you realise it has become the leading voice.
The cadenza lasts about three minutes. In Bach’s time a concerto movement rarely let one player go on alone for so long.

movements.heading: Affettuoso
movements.summary: “Tender, with feeling.” The string band is silent: only the three soloists play, like a trio in a small room. The flute, the violin and the harpsichord’s right hand each sing the same sighing tune in turn, while the harpsichord’s left hand plays the bass.

mainIdeas.name: The sighing tune
mainIdeas.description: a slow, falling melody in B minor, with small dotted rhythms.

mainIdeas.name: Imitation
mainIdeas.description: whatever one instrument sings, another repeats a moment later.

stops.hear: A soft, sad tune in the flute and the violin, with the harpsichord answering
stops.happening: The three soloists alone, in B minor

stops.hear: The tune passes from one instrument to another; each takes the lead and then steps back
The music moves through other keys and becomes more intense
The opening tune comes back in B minor

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: The three voices close softly together
stops.happening: The movement ends in the minor

notice: Bach wrote this movement for three players but four lines of music: the harpsichordist plays a melody with one hand and the bass with the other.

movements.heading: Allegro
movements.summary: A light, skipping finale. It begins like a [[fugue|fugue]]: one soloist plays the tune alone, and the others enter one by one with the same tune. A smoother middle section in B minor follows, and then the whole opening section comes back unchanged.

mainIdeas.name: The skipping tune
mainIdeas.description: quick and dance-like, with a lilting, bouncing rhythm.

mainIdeas.name: The middle section
mainIdeas.description: a longer-breathed melody in B minor, more singing than dancing.

stops.hear: One soloist plays a skipping tune on its own; a second enters with the same tune, then the harpsichord
stops.happening: A [[fugato|fugato]]: the soloists enter one by one

stops.hear: The string band joins in and the texture thickens
stops.happening: The full group takes up the tune

stops.hear: Smoother and darker: a new, singing melody in a minor key
stops.happening: The middle section, in B minor

stops.hear: The skipping tune returns on its own, exactly as at the start
stops.happening: The opening section is repeated in full

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: A bright, firm close in D major

notice: The last part is an exact repeat of the first. Listen for whether the players change anything the second time.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: Trevor Pinnock is both the harpsichord soloist and the director, so the cadenza is played by the person leading the performance. Lisa Beznosiuk plays a wooden Baroque flute, softer than a modern metal one, which keeps the balance with the violin and the harpsichord.

threads.title: The harpsichord’s rise
threads.body: It starts in the background, takes over the first movement, shares the second as an equal, and in the third enters the fugue as one of the three voices.

threads.title: One small band
threads.body: The orchestra is only a handful of strings. In the slow movement even they stop, and the concerto becomes chamber music.

threads.title: Imitation
threads.body: Everywhere one instrument says something, another repeats it: the duets of the first movement, the sighs of the second, the entries of the third.
